en: IX. The Consecration Ceremony. 1. The Ritual for the Preparation of the Disciples (*śiṣyādhivāsanavidhi*).

Then, in the colored powder mandala or within another mandala, having first performed the worship consisting of the preparation of the vases (*kalaśādhivāsana*), the placement of offerings, the five types of service (*pañcopacāra*), and so forth, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should prepare for initiation those other than the disciples already prepared—those who have been well-examined, who are free from defects such as pride, who have been refined by the lay vows (*upāsaka*) and the like, by extensive learning and so forth, who are devoted, and who are fit for undertaking the commitments (*saṃvara*) of Vajrasattva—even if they lack noble lineage, virtues, or beauty.
If they should become those who, through faith, are intensely devoted to the vow of Vajrasattva and have no other teachers in the Vajrayāna,
it was said by the Blessed One in the *Sārddhatriśatikā*:
"One should tolerate even those who are deformed, devoid of virtues, or lowly."
The ritual procedure for the mandala is authorized for all four assemblies as well.
For those who are devoted to their own trainings and whose minds delight in the Mahāyāna.
Thus:
"of the four assemblies" refers to the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen;
"the procedure" refers to the entry and so forth.

"Of those who are disciplined, devoted to that [practice], and whose souls delight in the Mahāyāna"— by this, he demonstrates that mental action (*manaskarma*) is the primary factor of this vehicle (*yāna*) for the sake of showing non-contradiction.

For even regarding an action that is inherently faulty (*prakṛtisāvadya*), the Blessed One has frequently declared and we have elucidated in works such as the *Āmnāyamañjarī* that there is no transgression (*anāpatti*) due to a particularity in the motivation (*samutthānaviśeṣa*).
And elsewhere it is said:
"There is no offense for one whose mind is virtuous, nor for one who acts out of affection and compassion."
Thus,
even that which is prohibited is permitted for the compassionate one who perceives the welfare [of others].
And thus it is said:

Furthermore, for one who has accumulated merit, great learning, and so forth, and who possesses a very firm conviction that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams and are of the single flavor of emptiness—for such a person, where even the slightest scent of contradiction could there be between the vows of a monk and those of a Vajradhara?
For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One:

"One should make the monk a Vajradhara"—this must necessarily be accepted. Otherwise, how could one reconcile the Vinaya teaching that a monk who, due to the simultaneous awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of both parties, sees a dream and experiences everything up to the pleasure of the two organs with an external woman who is also seeing the dream and experiencing the pleasure of union, remains free from transgression? This must be explained.

If, however, the location should be a haunt of wicked people, then even for him the secret initiation and the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) should be bestowed by means of the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
But in the absence of wicked people, it should be done by means of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) alone.

For a monk who lacks firm conviction in reality, even if he is faithful, the reception of the external initiation of wisdom is forbidden; otherwise, due to the loss of his previous vows, there would be great harm.

If, however, the guru is one whose meditation is stable, then he too should bestow the wisdom-consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*) upon that same knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*); and for the recipient, there is not even the suspicion of non-celibacy, because of the absence of physical action.
For him, moreover, the distinctions of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth are to be demonstrated through the recollection of the bliss previously experienced during his state as a householder.

Furthermore, regarding the guru’s own status as a monk, when bestowing the secret consecration and the others, everything that has been said should be applied accordingly; enough of this digression—let us speak of the subject at hand.

There, one, two, or many disciples who have been initiated into the mandala should be made to kneel upon the ground with their knees touching it and holding handfuls of flowers; they should be told: "The entry into the mandala is not for the sake of prosperity in this world alone, nor even for the sake of prosperity in the next world, but rather for the attainment of the perfection of the three bodies of the Tathāgata."

Having thus announced, "In this way, the two types of exaltation will be attained," he causes [the disciples] to enter his own body through the mouth, emerge from the *vajra*, and— having meditated on them as being consecrated by the Tathāgatas together with their Prajñās, who have entered through the mouth and been drawn forth by the rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart while residing in the lotus of the Prajñā— he seats them at the eastern gate of the mandala and has them request entry:
"O Great Passion, you alone are my Teacher, the sole deliverer from the ocean of existence, which is terrifying with its waves of death, birth, old age, sickness, and so forth."
I desire, O Great Lord, the firm method of great awakening;
grant me the commitment and the reality, and grant me the thought of awakening.
Grant me the Triple Refuge of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
O Protector, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.
Thus, by teaching [the words] "Mahārata," one is equal to Vajradhara.
*Naya* means the path;
*samaya* refers to mantra, tantra, mudrā, and so forth.
Some say that first one should cause them to undertake the poṣadha vows;
thereafter, having made a single disciple the principal one, [one should say]:
"Come, child, to this method of the practice of the mantras of the Mahāyāna."
I shall teach you correctly, for you are a worthy vessel for the Great Vehicle.
The Buddhas, arisen throughout the three times, who possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra mantras.
By means of this incomparable application of mantra, the great and most terrible army of Māra was shattered by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having conformed to worldly convention and having set the wheel of Dharma in motion, they have attained nirvāṇa;
therefore, my child, apply this mind toward the attainment of omniscience.
One should cause [the disciple] to undertake this by means of the recitation:
"This," [referring to] that which is inclined toward the method of mantra.
Then...
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds. I rejoice in the merit of the world and set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Thus one should have him recite it three times.

In this way, having granted the irreversible consecration (*avaivartyasatseka*) in the wheel so as to cause him who holds the general vows to receive the vows of an *ācārya*, [one says]: "O Lord, speak to me!"
The reality of the wheel and its deity, and the preparatory rites for the preceptor.
I shall always be the preceptor of the commitment of all Buddhas, the supreme secret vow, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having thus caused [the student] to make this specific request, one should cause them to generate the thought of awakening (bodhicitta):
"May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me! I, named so-and-so, from this moment until I sit upon the seat of awakening, generate the supreme, unsurpassed thought of awakening."
Just as the Lords of the three times have made their firm resolve for perfect enlightenment.
I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline: the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous qualities, and the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha with respect to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the supreme and unsurpassed Three Jewels.
I accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā according to reality;
and I shall accept the Ācārya in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the four gifts six times every day, within the worthy Mahāratnakula, at a delightful and auspicious time. (182)
I receive the True Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles—
within the pure Great Lotus family, which gives birth to great awakening.
I accept the restraint fully joined with all [deities] from every side,
performing acts of worship according to my ability within the exalted assembly of the Great Action Family.
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
and having undertaken the complete vow for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are not liberated;
I shall give comfort to those who are uncomforted; I shall establish all sentient beings in final nirvana.

Having thus caused [the disciple] to recite this three times—this has been explained in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*—one should then protect them with the *Amṛtakuṇḍalin* mantra. Then, having visualized the syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*, which are black, red, and white, situated upon the sun, sun, and moon, or the sun, moon, and moon, respectively, atop a vajra, lotus, and wheel at their heart, throat, and head; and while uttering those [syllables], one should touch the heart, throat, and head with the right fist joined with a vajra and scented water. One should offer a flower on the head, incense and a lamp before [the face], and again offer scent at the heart.

Thereafter, facing north, he should give to the disciples a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) made of *aśvattha* or other such wood, twelve finger-breadths long, straight, free of insects, unsplit, without blemishes, washed with fragrant water, and with a flower tied to its tip. They, facing either east or north within a four-cubit square maṇḍala smeared with cow dung and the like,
should recite "Oṃ vajrahāsa haṃ," chew it from the tip, and then, looking upward at where it has fallen, cast it away without regard, facing forward.
One should declare the future accomplishment for them according to the direction in which their tooth-stick falls:

if it falls toward the east, north, west, south, upward, or downward, there are respectively the accomplishments of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the state of a knowledge-holder (*vidyādhara*), or the underworld (*pātāla*).
However, if it falls outside the mandala, there is no accomplishment.

Thereafter, having given water consecrated with the syllable *vaṃ* and recited [the mantra] once for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), he should cause [the disciples] to drink three handfuls of scented water consecrated seven times with the *kuṇḍalinī* [mantra], while reciting: "Oṃ hrīḥ! O Pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person; remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ!

Then, having seated them outside, he should spread many *kuśa* grasses with unbroken tips, consecrated with the syllable *hūṃ* or recited over by the *kuṇḍalinī*, for the purpose of lying down; likewise, he should provide one *kuśa* blade born from the syllable *dhīḥ* and consecrated by that same *kuṇḍalinī* for the purpose of a pillow.
One should give [the thread] with the mantra: *oṃ vajratīkṣṇa vaṃ*.

Thereafter, a red thread the length of the disciple’s body, tripled, empowered seven times by the *hūṃ* syllable and the *kuṇḍalinī*, and tied with either three or six knots, should be placed on their right arm or left hand as stated in other tantras. Reciting: *oṃ buddha maitrī rakṣa rakṣa sarvān svāhā*, one should tie it oneself, properly protect it, and inspire them [with these words]:
"Whatever evil was committed in the past over many millions of eons..."
For all that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a maṇḍala.
The occurrence of all suffering and the miserable realms are destroyed for those whose minds are utterly pure regarding this supreme practice.
Today, O great-souled ones, you have obtained incomparable gains,
in that you have been [accepted] here into the teaching by all the Victors together with their sons.
All of you, as you are being born, have been taken up by great beings;
therefore, you shall indeed be well-born in the Mahāyāna.
This is the glorious, supreme path, the great success of the Mahāyāna; by means of it, you shall go forth and become Tathāgatas.
Having thus caused [them] to hear:
"being born" refers to the entry into the maṇḍala;
that which has its arising (*udaya*) in the Mahāyāna itself through a succession of great excellences.

Thereafter, having protected them with the Kuṇḍalī-mantra and having taught the Kuṇḍalī-mantra for the purpose of its recitation, one should say, "In the morning, you shall tell us your dream," and then have them sleep either inside a peaked house (kūṭāgāra) at the edge of the maṇḍala ground, screened by a curtain or the like, or elsewhere on a lion's couch.
One should enter the maṇḍala house oneself and recite the Kuṇḍalī-mantra for the sake of protection.
Here, that vow which is given even to one who does not act as an ācārya is the common [vow], characterized merely by going for refuge and generating the spirit of awakening (bodhicitta).
That which is bestowed for the purpose of making one an *ācārya* is the *ācārya-saṃvara*, which is comprised of the five families.
Therefore, this is the procedure for the consecration of the disciple (*śiṣyādhivāsanavidhi*), preceded by the bestowal of these two vows.
2. The Procedure for the Entrance of the *Ācārya*.

Thereafter, at dawn, the Guru, having offered the *bali* and emerged from the maṇḍala house, asks the disciples about their dreams. If an inauspicious dream is indicated by such signs as falling from a mountain, he protects them with the Kuṇḍalī mantra. At the time of entering the maṇḍala house, the disciples are encouraged [with the following]: "Oṃ, enter, O Blessed One, Great Bliss! Filled with liberation, bestower of the bliss of all accomplishments, supreme among the highest joys! Accomplish! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Be fully accomplished!

Thus encouraged, having entered and circumambulated, [the Guru], in the form of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*), stands at the western and other doors and [opens] the eastern and other doors of the maṇḍala.

Reciting "Oṃ vajrodghāṭaya samaya praveśaya hūṃ," he opens [the eyes] and [offers] the flower garland: "Oṃ, I bow to the Blessed One with intentions of supreme bliss and with most graceful, playful gestures: Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Hi hi hi hi hīḥ! O Lord, accept this handful of flowers: Hoḥ!"

Having cast [the garland] into the maṇḍala with this mantra, having taken it up again and bound it upon one’s own head, and having formed the resolve for the garland consecration (*mālābhiṣeka*), one should visualize the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*) and the Guru as becoming manifest. Having received from him the garland consecration and all the other consecrations to be described hereafter according to the ritual, and having obtained permission for all the activities of a master (*ācārya-karma*), one should, for the sake of admitting the disciples, desire the accomplishment of the maṇḍala preceded by a praise of reality consisting of wisdom and means whose nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
One should also perform the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
Because it is characterized by the arising of space, the supreme one is without beginning or end;
may the Great Being, composed of the great vajra, Akṣobhyavajra and the others, grant me accomplishment.
O supreme among all, great accomplishment, presiding deity of Maheśvarī!
O King who holds all vajras, may you, the supreme syllable, grant me success.
You are faultless and eternal, the one who inspires passion for all passions;
O Blessed One, as such, grant me accomplishment through the reality of Great Passion and Great Rapture.
The Tathāgata, the supreme dharma, utterly pure and liberated from the beginning;
Samantabhadra, the soul of all, O Bodhisattva—may you grant me success!
O supreme among all, through the great siddhi and the preeminent mudrā of Māheśvarī, may I be perfected by the great excellence of the Vajra; O Lord of Vajra-arrogance, [grant this] to me!
Pervading the minds of all sentient beings, abiding in the hearts of all sentient beings,
he is indeed the father of all sentient beings, the supreme object of desire for those who hold the supreme samaya.
By that truth through which true knowledge— the maṇḍala whose nature is wisdom and skillful means—
is attained, by that truth, O Protector, may you fulfill my desires.
All phenomena are like reflections; they are transparent, pure, and undisturbed.
They are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet they arise from causes and karma.
By this truth— that suchness is born from reality— may all the disciples, free from stain, clearly behold the reflection of the maṇḍala.
Reciting thus:
"Space is the sign and the example for arising"—the meaning is that Vajrasattva consists of emptiness and compassion because he is such [an essence].
"All vajras" refers to the body-vajra and the others.
Through all passions and all desires, he wins over sentient beings;
he is the Great Passion, the great compassion that is without objective support.
Primordially liberated through natural purity, the universal self whose nature is awakening by way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—such a being is a Bodhisattva.

*Kāma* means that which is desired; *agra* means foremost. For those who possess the summit of the occasion (*samayāgriṇām*), that is, for those possessing right knowledge (*samyagjñānavatām*), there are five words beginning with "pure" (*accha*), due to their being free from the obscurations of afflictions, the knowable, and meditative attainments, and due to their being beyond the scope of words such as "intrinsic nature. They are stainless because of their empowerment by truth and their empowerment by the Blessed One. This is the procedure for the entrance of the master. 3. The procedure for the bestowal of the water of the occasion.

Then, if the door-ācāryas are unwilling, or if they are willing for another [to do so], [the master] should have the disciple—who has been consecrated and who observes the two vows—bathed; having purified him with perfumes and other substances, he should dress him in red garments consecrated by the *kuṇḍalī* mantra, or otherwise, suspended outside the curtain (*kāṇḍapaṭa*) in the form of Vairocana or in the form of the Lord of the Maṇḍala.
Having performed the donning [of the garments] with: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānuttarabodhyalaṅkāravastrapūjāmeghasamudraspharaṇasamaye hūṃ*.
"Oṃ vajra rakṣa haṃ"— with this, the upper garment is donned. "Oṃ vajroṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ"— with this, the uṣṇīṣa is donned.
With a cloth that has been consecrated by the recitation of the *Amṛtakuṇḍalī* mantra, and which is either red or yellow,
one should bind the blindfold with the mantra: *oṃ cakṣurbandhaṃ varam ānaya hūṃ*.

Having recited "Āḥ Khaṃ Vīra Hūṃ," [the master] should question the candidate—who holds a garland of flowers, has offered the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), and has been sprinkled with water from the all-purpose vase—once he has been established at the eastern gate of the mandala by the Karma-vajrin for entry into the mandala, his body radiant with rays of light emanating from the black *Hūṃ*, red *Āḥ*, and white *Oṃ* syllables placed upon sun, moon, and sun disks atop the vajra-fists at his heart, throat, and head. [The master] should ask:
"Who are you, O lover of pleasure?"
He should say:

"I am fortunate; I am great bliss. Then, having caused him to generate the thought of awakening while reciting: "Oṃ, I generate the mind of all yoga," he should place the vajra with flowers upon his heart.
Reciting, "Oṃ surate samaya tvaṃ hoḥ sidhya vajra yathāsukham," and holding [the vajra], he says:
"Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
You must not speak of this supreme secret maṇḍala of all the Tathāgatas to anyone who has not entered the maṇḍala."
And having said, "This is not to be disbelieved," he draws [the deity] forth while reciting: *oṃ yamāntakṛt hūṃ*.

Oṃ, I offer myself for the service and worship of all Tathāgatas; O Vajrasattva of all Tathāgatas, empower me! Oṃ, I offer myself for the service and worship of all Buddhas; O Vajravairocana of all Tathāgatas, empower me!
In the south: Oṃ, I offer myself for the consecration of the worship of all Tathāgatas; O Vajraratna of all Tathāgatas, consecrate me!
In the west:
Oṃ, I offer myself for the performance of the worship of all Tathāgatas; O Vajradharma of all Tathāgatas, cause me to proceed!
In the north:

*Oṃ, for the sake of the ritual of worship of all Tathāgatas, I offer myself; O Vajrakarma of all Tathāgatas, act for me!* Having thus prostrated before the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, who reside in the maṇḍala, by means of these five mantras in their respective order, one should again [proceed] to the eastern gate.
"Oṃ, I offer myself for attendance upon the feet of the Guru.
Oṃ, I offer myself for the sake of protecting all sentient beings. Thus one should cause [the student] to recite, preceded by a comprehension of the meaning.
It has been stated by some that the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) attained within his heart, as well as other subsequent installations (*nyāsa*) starting from the heart,
should not be contemplated at this stage, for that constitutes a different ritual procedure.
Therefore—

"Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas; therefore, I shall generate in you the vajra-wisdom (*vajrajñāna*), by which wisdom you will attain even the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your samaya be violated. Having said this, he places the vajra on [the disciple's] head and, sounding the bell: "This is your samaya-vajra; it would shatter your head if you were to speak of this to anyone."
Having thus caused [him] to hear this and having placed the vajra upon his heart:
"Oṃ! Vajrasattva himself now resides within your heart;
if you should speak of this method, he will pierce it and depart in that very instant."
Having thus commanded, while holding the vessel with the ring finger and thumb, he pours the water situated above the *vijaya-kalaśa* into [the disciple’s] mouth, saying:
"This water of hell shall burn you for transgressing the pledge (*samaya*);
through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment. Drink this adamantine nectar-water!"
Having recited this and caused [the disciple] to drink from the vessel, [the master says]:
"From this day forward, I am your Vajrapāṇi; whatever I tell you to do, that must be performed by you."
And he should say: "You must not despise me,
lest you, by failing to avoid danger, should meet your end and fall into hell."
"Those" refers to you;
"hellish" means like the waters of the Vaitaraṇī river;
"vajra-amṛta water" means that it is a vajra by way of restraint and nectar by way of favor.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the water of commitment (samayodaka).
4. The Procedure for Possession:

Subsequently, prior to the time of the actual practice (*sādhana*), one should cause the deity to descend into the vessel or the disciple for the purpose of ascertaining success (*siddhi*) and so forth.

In that regard, first, having performed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) in a place favorable to the mind such as a mountain and so forth, one who possesses a steady mind should firmly take recourse in the yoga of Vajrasattva. Having attained the power of possession (*āveśa*), one should consecrate a disciple endowed with all the [auspicious] characteristics and, placing him before oneself, instantly—immediately after emptiness—generate him in the form of Amitābha arising from the syllable *Āḥ*. Then, saying, "May all the Tathāgatas empower him; may Vajrasattva enter me," one should visualize within his heart a yellow four-cornered earth-maṇḍala marked by a vajra born from *Laṃ*, upon which is a sun disk with a blue *Hūṃ*.
Having visualized a white syllable *haḥ* upon a moon within a white, circular Varuṇa-maṇḍala marked by a water-pot (*kalaśa*) at the head;
and a red syllable *āḥ* upon a moon within a blue wind-maṇḍala shaped like a bow and marked by two fluttering banners born from the syllable *yaṃ* at the throat.

Having summoned the Vajras of Mind, Body, and Speech with rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, one should cause them to be absorbed respectively into the syllables *hūṃ*, *haḥ*, and *āḥ* which constitute their essential nature. Then, while sounding the bell preceded by the offering of incense, one should meditate on the disciple being lifted up by the red syllable *jhaiḥ* situated upon a triangular fire-maṇḍala—which is red, marked with the letter *raṃ*, transformed from the wind-maṇḍala ignited beneath the feet, and radiating beams of light—and whose entire body is being filled by the rays of the syllables *hūṃ* and so forth that have entered through the hollows of the feet via the mass of rays from the syllable *jhaiḥ*.
"ĀVEŚAYA STOBHAYA RA RA RA RA CĀLAYA CĀLAYA HŪṂ HAḤ ĀḤ JHAIḤ. Reciting this mantra one hundred times while intent on meditation, one should cause [the deity] to enter.

If, once possessed, [the disciple] leaps far upward, then one should visualize a Mount Meru made of vajra above him, above that the maṇḍala of Mahendra, above that a yellow five-pronged vajra, above that the syllable YAḤ, and above that Vairocana; having visualized this, one should bring him back down.

When such possession has occurred, one should visualize the Vajra of Speech, consisting of the seed-syllable, being impelled by the light-rays from the seed-syllable of the disciple’s mind-vajra; and having visualized on the tongue the red syllable ĀḤ, situated upon a moon and surrounded by garlands of flames, one should say, "Speak, O Vajra!
Thus, he will truthfully declare whatever task pertains to himself or another, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

Then, having drawn in the deity who has descended by means of the light-rays from one's own heart and causing her to be absorbed within the seed-syllable in one's heart, one should hold a vajra at the crown of the disciple's head and dismiss [the deity] with "Oṃ kṛto vaḥ" and so forth, followed by "Hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ mur.
Alternatively, [one may do so] according to what was written by Ghaṇṭāpāda.
A cloth from a woman stained with menstrual blood, sprinkled with feces, urine, and the like,
crushed together with excrement and mixed with guggulu resin;
Having taken up the fire of the hungry ghosts (pretānala) and placed it in a lotus vessel,
he should cast all of that into it while standing in the ālīḍha posture.
The Wielder of the Vajra, possessed by wrath and embodying the three wheels, should then offer incense to that one who is the essence of the triple wheel; he will undoubtedly become possessed.
"Stay, O Great Wrathful One! HŪṂ! We know Śrī Heruka; we meditate upon the King of Vidyās, svāhā!"—with this, one should impel the Hero.

Thus, according to the procedure taught in the *Lakṣyābhidhāna-tantra*, one should cause [the deity] to enter. [The body] is sprinkled with the ten "lamps of nectar," such as feces, urine, and so forth.

The Guru, in the form of Saṃvara, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, should fumigate the disciple—who stands in the *ālīḍha* posture as the very essence of Saṃvara with palms joined at the heart—with his right hand while reciting the mantra beginning with "tiṣṭha" (stand! along with the sound of a bell held in his left hand, doing so with great solemnity. Then, it should be understood whether [the disciple] is possessed or not, and so forth; even though this may be found in some tantras.

It has been stated that one should invoke the deity by placing before [the altar] a girl twelve years of age whose virginity is intact and whose primary and secondary limbs are unimpaired, and likewise a youth of the same age who is ignorant of the female sphere and whose primary and secondary limbs are unimpaired. Nevertheless, for a guru of accumulated merit who possesses the power of firm meditative cultivation (*dṛḍhabhāvanā*), the deity may descend instantly upon a worthy recipient— even if he is physically unimpaired, advanced in years, and experienced in sexual intercourse— [provided he appears] moment after moment as the very embodiment of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (*vajrabhṛt*).
Thus, because it has been extensively revealed in other tantras, one should strive for the purpose of the disciple’s possession; this is the procedure for possession (āveśavidhi).
5. The procedure for the entry of the blindfolded disciple (āndhapaṭa-śiṣyapraveśavidhi).

Then, having asked the disciple facing the mandala, "What kind of appearance do you perceive with your eyes?", and having ascertained his suitability for the rites of pacification, enrichment, subjugation, or the violent rites (*abhicāra*) according to the sequence of the white, yellow, red, or black appearances he describes, the master should take him by both thumbs with his right hand holding a vajra. While performing the *vajrapada* dance and reciting the *kuṇḍali* mantra, he should cause him to circumambulate three times to the right and perform the "empowerment of truth" (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) as follows:
"Thus, this disciple has been properly introduced into the mandala by me."
May the lineage of these deities be as meritorious as that [of yours].
Whatever kind of accomplishment he may attain, in whatever lineage he may be a vessel,
and whatever the power of his merit may be— may that very same thing be his within this mandala.
Thus concludes the procedure for the entrance of the disciple behind the curtain into the maṇḍala.

6. The procedure for the garland empowerment (*mālābhiṣeka*): Then, having previously taken up a garland consecrated with the syllable *trāṃ*, one should pluck a single fresh, small flower and place it in the joined palms of the disciple.

Then, having resolved that flower-garland as being himself and having been purified of all stains by means of the three-syllable mantra, he should—being thus empowered by the Guru and preceded by devotion—rely upon the Lord of the Maṇḍala, who stands before him as if present within the circle of the assembly; and having mentally entered that Maṇḍala, he should place the flower upon his head.

"Oṃ, stay! O Vajra, be firm for me; be eternal for me. Empower my heart; bestow upon me all accomplishments! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ, accept this handful of flowers, O Lord! Hoḥ! Reciting this mantra, one should designate the practitioner's *kula* according to where the flower falls within the five lines, and should grant the corresponding yoga and observe the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
If a flower falls upon the *ūrṇā*, the head, or the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Buddhas, there is the accomplishment of the *mahāmudrā*;
if it falls on the eyes or the mouth, there is the accomplishment of the mantra;
and if it falls on the crown of the head (*uttamāṅga*), it is the highest [accomplishment].
In the middle part it is middling; in the lower part it is inferior;
and when very far from the image, it is delayed.
Success is swiftly attained in their proximity.
As for the deities, however, one’s own station must be known by distinguishing it according to the [specific] compartments and so forth.
If [the flower] falls between two deities, then whichever deity the flower is closer to, that deity's family belongs to the practitioner.
But when there is equality, both rules are established. Then, whichever [side] he prefers is his family. If it falls outside the five lines, one should throw again, up to three times.
In that case, if one falls outside [the boundary], there is only a minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*).
There is no accomplishment at all within the outer circular lines or outside the outer circle of vajras.
Furthermore, one must not show this mandala to others.
Having rendered him fit through the recitation of mantras and other means, he should be introduced on another occasion;
for it is said that [the disciple] falls into the interior of the outer vajra-garland.
Then, taking that flower, let it be fastened to the garland.
Reciting, "Oṃ, accept this being, O Mahābala," one should bind [the garland] upon the head of the disciple. This is the procedure for the garland consecration (mālābhiṣeka).

In this context, even when flowers fall upon deities made of colored powder (*rajas*), there is no fault for one who possesses a virtuous mind; thus, there is no defect whatsoever. However, regarding an unlearned person, it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* that since the colored powder would be disturbed by the falling of flowers upon a powder-mandala (*rajo-maṇḍala*), demerit (*apuṇya*) might arise; therefore, the flower should be cast upon the emblem located on the victory-vase (*vijaya-kalaśa*).
When this possession has occurred, after explaining the auspicious and other results,
one should stabilize the possession with "Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra," perform the inquiry regarding the appearance of the eyes and so forth up to the binding of the head, and then dismiss the descended deity.

However, they say that because [the disciple] lacks the capacity for the rite of entry (*āveśavidhi*) when it has not been performed, one should conduct the inquiry regarding the appearance before the eyes and so forth immediately after the offering of the water of the pledge (*samayodaka*).
7. Regarding the procedure for entry consisting of vision:
thereupon, having visualized the Lord within the moon at the heart of the disciple, the letter *repha* on the forehead, and two flaming *oṃ*s in the two eyes;
Today Vajrasattva himself, intent on opening your eyes,
opens for you the unsurpassed vajra-eye, which perceives all things.
Reciting "Oṃ jñānacakṣuḥ hūṃ āḥ svāhā," one should remove the blindfold.
Because he possesses all eyes and the quality of seeing everything, he is the Vajra Eye, an eye that is unimpeded toward all forms.
Because it removes obscurations like that of the Buddhas, it is unsurpassed.

Then, having said, "Behold Hevajra," and having first stated the names of the deities, one should show them—beginning with the Lord of the Maṇḍala and proceeding as appropriate up to the guardian of the northern gate or Sumbharāja—saying:
"Behold this very maṇḍala now with the force of faith."
And you, born into the family of the Buddhas, are empowered by mudrās and mantras.
Through this perfection, you shall become the foremost of all accomplishments and the supreme of commitments;
perform the worship of mantras with the graceful union of the vajra and the lotus.
Having recited thus:
"I have entered the great mandala of the Vajra-maṇḍala;
I have been shown the great mandala of the Yoga-maṇḍala."
I have been initiated into the secret maṇḍala and the great maṇḍala.
Having thus caused [the disciple] to recite, one should cause them to recite the pledge:
"Hoḥ! Hoḥ! Hoḥ!
This is the ritual procedure for the entry of the disciple into the maṇḍala consisting of the vision [of it].
8. The Ritual for the Water Consecration (Udakābhiṣeka-vidhi):

Thereafter, for the sake of the water consecration, having given a teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one’s means, with knees placed upon the ground and palms joined in reverence, [one should pray:
"Just as the great festival was bestowed by Bodhivajra upon the Buddhas..."
For the sake of my protection as well, O Khavajra and others, grant it to me now!
Reciting thus, he should make the request.

Then the Guru, outside the root mandala, so that he is not touched by the bathing water, should perform the *nīrājana* for the disciple—who has been visualized in the form of Vajradhara and is facing the mandala—at the pedestal and so forth, which has been previously prepared for the purpose of the image bath, beginning with "a double lotus (*viśvapadma*) in the eastern direction facing the entrance door" and ending with "the mandala visualized upon the seat. He should do so according to the previously mentioned sequence of *nīrājana*: *oṃ āḥ vighna...* and so forth.
Thereafter, having worshipped the Tathāgatas and the Vidyā-devis residing in the infinite directions with rays from the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*), for the sake of the disciple’s consecration:
"Just as the consecration of the Buddhas was bestowed by the Vajrī for the protection of the world as a mine of virtues, so indeed do you bestow it upon this one."

Having thus supplicated with this verse, those Tathāgatas, having entered into wisdom and melted through great passion, enter within by way of the Vairocana-gate; emerging through the path of the vajra, they are introduced into the lotus of the Goddess by her mouth with those fluids.

Instantly, immediately following the [meditation on] emptiness, the disciple is consecrated as having the form of Akṣobhya together with Prajñā, born from the *hūṃ*-vajra and non-different from the Jñānasattva. Then, emerging from the lotus through forms possessing arms, faces, and so forth, and filling the sky, they remain together with the Vidyās such as Locanā and the others, accompanied by showers of parasols, banners, flags, garments, musical instruments, songs, dances, flowers, saffron, and the like. With white flasks filled with the nectar of bodhicitta held in bud-like hands, those goddesses such as Rūpavajrā and the others consecrate that disciple who has emerged from the lotus.

May that auspiciousness which belongs to Great Bliss— the one who dwells in the hearts of all sentient beings, who is the self of all, the sovereign of all excellent families, and the progenitor of all beings— be yours today at this supreme consecration.
May that Buddha— who possesses the splendor of Mount Kāñcana, who is the lord of the three worlds, who has abandoned the three stains,
and whose eyes are like the petals of a blossomed lotus— grant you today this auspiciousness that brings peace.
May that which was taught by him— the eminent, unshakable, and renowned one, honored by men and gods throughout the three worlds,
the supreme Dharma that brings peace to all beings— be an auspicious omen for you today, bringing peace.
May that Saṅgha— endowed with the True Dharma, rich in the auspiciousness of learning, worthy of offerings from humans, gods, and asuras, the abode of glory,
and the most eminent among assemblies— be today the auspiciousness that brings peace to you.

Thus, while auspiciousness is being ushered in by songs of benediction, and having himself sung those [songs], he should draw a little bit from each of the jars such as the *vijaya* jar and so forth, and having placed it in a lotus vessel or a conch shell—or first from the *vijaya* jar—uttering: "Oṃ! By means of the empowerment of Great Bliss Vajrasattva, I empower you; may you become firm as the sovereign of all Tathāgatas," even if he does not recite it because of his preference for brevity.
With the right hand in a fist grasping a vajra with leaves,
[one should perform the sprinkling] first from the vases of the four Tathāgatas, then from the vases of the four goddesses,
and then, as appropriate, from the vases of the maṇḍala deities.

And in the absence of the victory flask (vijayakalaśa), [I perform] the consecration with water consisting of Akṣobhya, in the form of the nectar of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), dripping from the tip of a vajra together with sprouts:
"I bestow the Great Vajra consecration, honored by the three realms,
which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all Buddhas."
Reciting "Oṃ āḥ, consecrate with the vajra-water, hūṃ; you are passion, I am passion," one should perform the consecration.
One should then contemplate that he has entered into the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the water consecration (udakābhiṣeka).
9. The Ritual Procedure for the Crown Consecration (mukuṭābhiṣeka):

Then, one should visualize [the disciple]—having been requested by the gurus with the words "Then, by means of the Bodhi-vajra," and so forth—as Ratnasambhava in the form of Āṃ-ratnajara, unified with the Jñānasattva, being consecrated by the Tathāgata goddesses stationed in the sky with vases, and being presented with auspicious songs by Rūpavajrā and the others. One should meditate [upon this].
The same applies to the empowerments of the names of the Vajra-lords.

Then, [the master] places upon the crown of the disciple’s head a crown fashioned from gold, cloth, and so forth, produced from Ratnasaṃbhava, having that very nature, and empowered by the five Tathāgatas in the form of Jñānasattvas who reside as the lords of the family in the center, on the forehead, on both sides, on the top of the head, and at the back, respectively:
*oṃ vajradhātvīśvari abhiṣiñca hūṃ*.
Oṃ sattvavajri abhiṣiñca bhrūṃ!
Oṃ ratnavajri abhiṣiñca āḥ!
Oṃ dharmavajri abhiṣiñca hrīḥ!

"Oṃ karmavajri abhiṣiñca trāṃ. Having thus performed [the rite] with these five mantras, while placing [the crown] upon the head, one recites the verse beginning with "The great vajra empowerment... and: "Oṃ āḥ, empower me with the vajra-crown hūṃ;
you are passion, I am passion."
Having recited thus, one should please [the deity] while reciting "vajra tuṣya hoḥ. This is the procedure for the crown consecration (mukuṭābhiṣeka).
10. The Ritual for the Vajra Empowerment:
Thereafter, one should bind a turban upon the forehead with the mantra *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ*.

Then, having visualized the disciple—who has thus made his request—as Amitābha, transformed from the syllable *hrīḥ* and the lotus, inseparable from the Jñānasattva, and having likewise visualized the vajra as being of the nature of Amitābha, one recites the verse beginning with "The Great Vajra Empowerment" (*abhiṣekaṃ mahāvajram*).
Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration;
take this, which is the state of all Buddhas, as the vajra for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
Reciting this, and having touched the heart, throat, and head of the disciple with the vajra, he should place it in the disciple’s right hand.
This is the procedure for the vajra-consecration.
11. The procedure for the bell-consecration.

Thereafter, having given the bell—which is the transformation of Amoghasiddhi—to his left hand, [the preceptor] causes him, who has thus requested [initiation], to assume the gesture of embracing the mudrā with both hands joined by the vajra and bell; then, preceded by the recitation of the verse beginning with "Abhiṣeka," he says: "Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Lord of Vajras; abide, O Vajra, you are the Samaya.
Having recited this, he says: "Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe aḥ aḥ! You are accepted, O Blessed One; be present within me!"
Thus ends the procedure for the bell-consecration, also known by the name of the consecration of sovereignty.
12. The procedure for the name-consecration:

Following that, having visualized the candidate—who has thus made his request—as the form of Vairocana born from the *oṃ* syllable, of one flavor with the *jñānasattva*, and while sounding the vajra and bell upon his head, one recites the verse beginning with "The consecration... and so forth.

"Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I consecrate you with the vajra-name-consecration as 'Vajradveṣa' or 'Vajramoha,' and so forth, or according to the name of one's own family following the falling of the flower, one should consecrate [the disciple] as the essence of Vairocana.
In that regard, the names of Vajrasattva are: Parama, Ādya, Anupama, Surata, Samarasa, Vijaya, Lalita, Sattva, Mahāsukha, Anaṅga, Jñāna, Sahaja, and Vajra.
The word 'vajra' should be connected to each [of these]."
In the names of the six Tathāgatas themselves:
for Akṣobhya, they are *hāsa-vilāsa-rati-līlā-lalita-svayambhū-dveṣa-hṛt-karuṇā-citta-hūṃkāra-akṣobhya-vajras*;
for Vairocana, they are *vajrocan-oṃkāra-śāśvata-tathāgata-māyā-buddha-rūpakāya-vajras*.
Of Ratnasambhava: Ratna, Cintāmaṇi, Kha, Gaganatejas, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Māna, and Vajra.
Of Amitābha: Rāga, Avalokita, Dharma, Padmavajrāṅkura, Padmāṅkura, Suratāṅkura, Karuṇāṅkura, Paramānanda, Suratānanda, Amita, and Vāgvajra.
Of Amoghasiddhi: Amogha, Parama, Aśva, Samaya, Pāramitā, Karma, Anila, Sparśa, and Īrṣyāvajra.
For Vajrasattva, [the consorts] are Vajravegī, Vajravilāsinī, Vajramadā, Vajrakaṅkaṇā, Vajrānanā, Vajrapatākā, Vajramālā, and Vajrodayā.
For Akṣobhya, they are Vajranairātmyā, Vajrahastā, Vajrāvalī, Vajrakarā, Vajramāmakī, and Dveṣarati. For Vairocana, they are Vajraḍākinī, Vajragaurī, Vajralāsyā, Vajralocanā, and Moharati.
The consorts of Ratnasambhava are Vajrahārā, Vajrāśvāsā, Vajrajvālā, Vajramālā, Vajrākāśā, and Ākāśarati.
The consorts of Amitābha are Vajrarāgā, Vajragītā, Vajrahomukhā, Vajravettālī, Vajramatī, Vajrahāsyā, Vajrapāṇḍarā, and Rāgarati.
The consorts of Amoghasiddhi are Vajragarvā, Vajramāyā, Vajravaḍavā, Vajratārā, Vajranarteśvarī, Samayavajrā, and Vajrarati.
The Ritual of the Name Empowerment (nāmābhiṣeka).

These six empowerments, beginning with the garland and water empowerments, are called the "empowerments of knowledge" (*vidyābhiṣeka*) because they produce the fitness that is the antidote to ignorance.
A disciple who has been sprinkled with these empowerments becomes authorized for the hearing, explanation, and mantra-practice of the Kriyā and Caryā Tantras.

"Even for the *Yoga* and *Yoginī* tantras"—this is the opinion of the Master [Abhayākaragupta], who considers it to be without scriptural authority (*anāgamam*). For nowhere has the Blessed One taught, nor is it logical, that the nature of those [higher initiations] can be described without the innate initiation (*sahaja-seka*) and its vow (*saṃvara*). Furthermore, these initiations are bestowed preceded by the granting of the common vow for those who do not desire the master initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), but for those who do desire it, they are bestowed preceded by both vows.
13. The Ritual for Bestowing the Three Samayas: Then, to that disciple who has offered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and joined his palms in reverence, [the master says]:
"O Treasure of Compassion, please bestow upon me the Vajrācārya initiation."
May I be capable of accomplishing the welfare of both myself and others through your grace.
Having recited this and performed the supplication to the Guru, one should meditate upon Vajra—the essence of *hūṃ*, the form of Vajrasattva—[with these words]:
"The Being without beginning or end, Vajrasattva, the Great Joy;
Samantabhadra, the Self of all, the Lord of the Vajra-pride, the Sovereign."
The Blessed One is the primordial, supreme person.
Reciting thus, one should cause [the disciple] to grasp it in its true nature.
Thus is the Vajra-samaya, the Lord of the World.
Then, having meditated upon the bell as born from the syllable ĀḤ—
This is that bell of all the Buddhas, known as the follower of sound;
you too must always hold it, for supreme awakening is what the Victors have deemed it to be.
Reciting thus, he should cause [the student] to grasp it in its true nature;
for, accompanied by a sound that flows effortlessly, the bell is like the wisdom of a Buddha,
while the disciple follows it.
For existence is pure by its very nature, yet it is rendered non-existent by [conceptualizing] natures;
through beings who are truly pure by nature, supreme existence is brought about.
Saying this, one should sound [the bell]. "By means of superimposed intrinsic natures, it is rendered as having contradictory existence"—this is the *ghaṇṭā-samaya*.
Thereafter, that...
Indeed, the mudrā is declared to be the *samaya* because of the firmness of the mental form;
since it makes all forms firm, it is therefore celebrated as "mudrā."
Thus,
having empowered the gnosis-seal (jñānamudrā), accomplish all siddhis through the enjoyment of all desires.

Having thus established [the disciple], one should empower the Gnosis-Seal (jñānamudrā) as the form of Vajrasattva through the method of union (sampuṭakrama) and cause him to perform the gesture of embracing.
As it is said in the Paramādya Tantra:
"One should grasp the vajra with the Reality (tattva) and sound the bell with the Dharma."
At that time, having empowered the mahāmudrā, one should recite [the mantra] at the heart.
Thus concludes the pledge of the mudrās.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for bestowing the three pledges.
14. The Ritual for the Initiation of the Master (Ācāryābhiṣekavidhi).

Thereafter, having seated [the candidate]—who has previously undertaken the three pledges—either in the bathing mandala or elsewhere visualized in that manner, one should contemplate him in the form of Vajrasattva. Then, according to the procedure described for the water initiation, from the seed-syllable at the heart down to the [water] dripping from the tip of the vajra, one performs the initiation: "The Great Vajra, honored by the three realms."
I bestow [this] which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.

Reciting "Oṃ āḥ, for the glory of the commitment of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ svāhā," one should perform the empowerment. Then, having visualized [the deity] with Akṣobhya as his crown, one should cause the other Tathāgata goddesses to enter that very form of the wisdom-being (jñānasattva). [Then recite]: "Oṃ supratiṣṭhita vajre svāhā."
Having empowered [the consort] with this mantra, one should offer flowers and other offerings to her.
Thus it has been said:
"Embracing a sixteen-year-old Prajñā with both hands..."
Through the union of the bell and the vajra, the consecration by the preceptor is considered [the fourth].
Thus, in brief, this peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) is the essential nature of Vairocana; this is the reality and purification of the maṇḍala.
In summary, the five aggregates are the five Buddhas.
By such statements as these, the reality (*tattva*) and purification (*viśuddhi*) of the deities are established;

however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), even in both stages of the mandala and so forth, reality and purification consist of the very nature of selflessness (*naiḥsvābhāvyātmikā*),
which is nothing other than suchness (*tathatā*).

One should explain the preparation of the master, including the drawing of the mandala with its retinue (saparikaramaṇḍalalikhanādi). Thus, the attainment of proficiency—consisting of the knowledge of the reality of the mandala and so forth, the non-transgression of the form of the samaya, and likewise the fulfillment of the vows (saṃvara) comprising what is to be done and what is not to be done—is said to be "fitness" (bhavyatā).

However, the reality of the mandala and other such matters have been described by us in detail in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*; this concludes the procedure for the Master Initiation (ācāryābhiṣeka), which has the alternative name "Irreversible Initiation" (avaivartyābhiṣeka).
15. The Procedure for the Bestowal of the Mantra.
Then, having himself recited the heart-mantra and other mantras one hundred and eight times, or three times:
"O Blessed One, you have been given by me; be present here!"
Saying this, he should give [the mantra] to the disciple.
The disciple also [should say]:
"O Blessed One, you are grasped by me; be present within me."
Having grasped [the bell] with this [verse], one should recite it three times.
This is the procedure for the offering of the mantra.
This very [procedure] is called the "mantra-consecration" (mantrābhiṣeka) by Ghaṇṭāpāda in other tantras such as the *Buddhakapāla*.

16. Regarding the procedure for applying collyrium: thereafter, having placed collyrium made of ghee and honey into a vessel of gold or silver, and using a golden applicator stick, one should visualize the syllable *praṃ* at the disciple’s eyes and, while reciting: “Oṃ, O Vajranetra, remove the cataract! Hrīḥ! apply the collyrium.
O child, the veil of ignorance has been removed from you by the Victors,
just as the King of Physicians removes the cataracts of the world with his probe.
Thus one should say:
"It has been removed," because its fitness for removal has been brought about.
This is the procedure for applying collyrium.
17. The Ritual for the Mirror Consecration:
Then, taking up a mirror and showing it to the disciple while it has been consecrated with the syllable *Āḥ*, [the teacher says]:
"All phenomena are like reflections; they are clear, pure, and undisturbed."
They are ungraspable and inexpressible, arising from causes and karma.
Like a mirror, O Vajrasattva, you are clear, pure, and unclouded;
for within your heart, my child, dwells the Lord of all Buddhas himself.

Having thus understood that all phenomena are indeed devoid of intrinsic nature and without abode, perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings; for you have been born upon the breast of the Protectors.
Thus one should say:
it is "clear" (accha) because of the absence of the turbidity of afflictions;
it is "pure" (śuddha) because of the lack of obscuration regarding the objects of knowledge.

It is "unclouded" because of the removal of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of those two. The first verse [refers] to natural purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*), while the second refers to purity from defilement (*vaimalyaviśuddhi*). He abides in those qualities by way of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), as an object of attainment (*prāpya*), as an objective support (*ālambana*), and by way of fitness (*yogyatā*).
Thus concludes the ritual for the mirror-consecration.
By stating the two rituals for the viewing of the mirror, [the author] has not merely looked at Ārya Nāgabuddhipāda’s *Maṇḍalopāyikā*.
However, some state that the procedure for the second visualization is taught with the intention of [describing] the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Then follows the procedure for the shooting of arrows: having recited "Hoḥ," one gives the bow produced from the syllable *hoḥ*.
One should say, "May you please all the Tathāgatas.

And at the time of casting the arrows, while the disciple recites, "I please all the Tathāgatas," four arrows should be cast in the four directions with the intention of piercing away obstacles, one upward and another downward; such is the procedure for casting the arrows.

19. The Procedure for the Secret Empowerment (*guhyābhiṣeka-vidhi*): Then, having made the place secluded with a curtain (*kāṇḍapaṭa*) and other such means, the disciple, having presented to the Guru for the sake of the secret empowerment a consort (*prajñā*) endowed with fresh youth and so forth—either a *samayinī* or, if she is unavailable, another—should join his palms in reverence and, visualizing the Guru as Vajrasattva, say:
"By the grace of your feet, I have attained the unsurpassed practice."
Therefore, O Lord, grant your favor by means of the secret empowerment.
Thus one should request with this verse.

Then the Guru, possessing the ego-identity of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*), having first performed the purification of the vajra and lotus, enters into union with her—who has assumed the form of a goddess immediately following the emptiness of her former ordinary female form—while reciting:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Reciting thus, one should visualize the Tathāgatas—Vairocana and the others—who have entered through the eyes and other sense organs via the rays of light from the heart-seed syllable, as having dissolved into oneself through the gate of Vairocana. Contemplating that they emerge through the *avadhūtī* after having melted by means of great passion (*mahārāga*), one stabilizes the innate (*sahaja*) [bliss] within the *vajramaṇi*. Having pressed the *vajramaṇi* with the thumb and ring finger and drawn it out from the lotus, one should resolve that this fluid of the Tathāgata is non-different from one’s own bodhicitta. Then, lest there be any suspicion of impurity due to seeing the disciple who is in the form of the *vāgvajra*, one should ensure it is not within the range of the disciple's vision by binding him with a blindfold.
O son of the Buddha, just as you were sprinkled by Vajradhara and the others in the past,
so do I sprinkle you, my child, with the beautiful thought of awakening.
Thus, reciting the mantra of the Lord of the Maṇḍala—

*oṃ āḥ vajradhṛk hūṃ*, and so forth— according to the specific tantra, one should cause [the disciple] to fall; this too is done with the thought that [the disciple] is the assembly of all Tathāgatas, such as Vairocana and the rest.
Saying, "Aho! Great Bliss!", he should drink.
Then, the Wisdom Consort, having risen while remaining naked, should place drops of the nectar of the Tathāgata situated within her own lotus into his mouth.
He too should drink in that manner.
Thus, because it is performed with the two secrets—the conventional bodhicitta of both wisdom and means—it is called the "Secret Empowerment. This is the procedure for the Secret Empowerment.
20. The Procedure for the Wisdom-Knowledge Empowerment.

Thereafter, when the disciple—whether that same woman or another, established in the commitments and vows, and endowed with beauty and youth—has made this request with the verse beginning "By means of the Bodhi-vajra," [the teacher says]:
"This delightful dhāraṇī of yours is to be cultivated; it was devised by the Buddhas.
Through the application of the sequence of the wheel, partake in the true bliss."
While in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, one should gaze at the mind as it resides within the jewel.
Having thus explained this, he should offer it.
She too, displaying a lotus—a garment made fragrant with saffron and other perfumes—should say to the disciple:
"O, my lotus is endowed with all happiness!"
I stand before him who serves according to the prescribed rule.
O Padmā, perform whatever tasks are required, such as the propitiation of the Perfectly Awakened One;
for the King of Great Bliss himself is always established right here.
One should say: "Bhaja mokṣa hoḥ.

He too, being himself the form of the deity, having produced the Goddess Prajñā in her divine form, should visualize the filaments and gems of the lotus and thunderbolt generated by *hrīḥ* and *hūṃ*, and the yellow syllable *phaṭ* produced from *āḥ* and *oṃ* at the vajra-mouth. Then, having moved the channel located in the left-left limb with the forefinger marked by the red syllable *hrīḥ* and with the tongue, preceded by the sound *śīṭ*, he should draw her forth.
Oṃ śī śī śī ha ha ha svāhā. Thus:
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra, which is the passion of all Tathāgatas.

Thus reciting the mantra and having his body empowered by the Tathāgatas and others drawn forth by the rays from the seed-syllable in his own heart— as understood through the teacher’s instruction— he, having become of one flavor with the infinite Vairocana, Locanā, and the rest who have been introduced by the teacher, should commence the rati. Through contact with the Prajñā, the glorious one should perceive the reality (*tattva*),
while gazing at the mind situated within the jewel [of the *uṣṇīṣa*] from the vajra-paryaṅka posture.

Having reflected thus and having sustained [the state] according to one's ability, one should slowly release [it], extract it from the lotus with the tongue itself, and drink the *bodhicitta*—which is the nature of the *samaya*—with the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*).

"The wheel" (*cakra*) refers to the circle of deities such as Vairocana together with the consort; its "application in sequence" (*krameṇa prayoga*) consists of the bringing forth, the entry, and the emergence via the path of the *vajra*.
"The ritual procedure" (*vidhāna*) refers to the production of the forms of the goddesses and so forth.
Regarding "liberation" (*mokṣa*): liberation, which is the absence of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and the supreme form of the deity, must be explained by the Guru.
Reality (*tattva*) is the inconceivability of all phenomena; because it conforms to their reflection, the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), whose nature is innate bliss, is called reality.
Mind (*citta*) is the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
The jewel belongs to the vajra;
if a woman is being consecrated, then the jewel belongs to the lotus. "Beholding" means looking—that is, making one's gaze into that [object] while beholding it.
This is the procedure for the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*).
21. The Procedure for the Fourth Empowerment:
Immediately thereafter, one should bestow the fourth empowerment by means of speech alone.

One should explain that very wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), which is the sprouted *bodhicitta*, increasing through meditative cultivation, having attained freedom from obscuration, whose nature is the reality (*tattva*) of the inconceivability of all phenomena, and whose essence is the Great Vajradhara consisting of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) endowed with the seven limbs; this is the form of the fourth empowerment. Thus concludes the procedure for the fourth empowerment.
22. The Ritual for Bestowing the Knowledge-Vow (Vidyāvratadānavidhi):

Immediately thereafter, having placed the hand of that Prajñā into the hand of the disciple, and holding those two [hands] with his own left hand, he places his right hand, which holds a vajra, upon the head of the disciple, saying: "You are witnesses here; she has been offered by me to him."
Thus, having made the Tathāgatas your witnesses:
there is no other means for attaining pure Buddhahood, nor is this triple world ever free from it;
therefore, never at any time be separated from this.
This is that unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
the fool who transgresses it shall not attain supreme accomplishment.
Saying this, he should bestow the *vidyāvrata*.
This is the procedure for bestowing the *vidyāvrata*. 5.
23. The Procedure for the *Vajravrata*.
Thereafter, having visualized the disciple in the form of Vajrasattva:
"This very state of all Buddhas resides in the hand of Vajrasattva;
you too must always uphold it, the firm vow of Vajrapāṇi."

Reciting thus, he should cause [the disciple] to take hold of the vajra. He [the disciple] should recite: *oṃ sarvatathāgatasiddhivajrasamaya tiṣṭha eṣa tvāṃ dhārayāmi vajrasattva hīḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ*.
Reciting thus, one should take it up.
This is the ritual procedure for the Vajra-vow.
24. The Ritual for Bestowing the Śaryāvratas:
Then, having recited three times over the khaṭvāṅga, ḍamaru, and lotus vessel with the heart-mantra of any one [deity] such as Buddhakapāla, Saṃvara, or Hevajra, [the master] says:
"Therefore, O Hero, take this khaṭvāṅga, ḍamaru, and bowl."
This is the mudrā of Śrī Vajrasattva, abiding both externally and internally.
Reciting this verse, one should cause [the disciple] to take [the items].

Or, regarding other limbs of conduct (*caryāṅga*) mentioned in other tantras—other than the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and so forth—one should cause them to be taken with the words "Take that which has been consecrated by the heart-mantra of the respective Lord of the Mandala," and so on.
And thus it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*:
One should cause a great image to be made, resembling the color white, wearing a crown of matted locks,
and entirely conforming to the vows and observances of the mantra.
One should consume all food and edibles consisting of bulbs, roots, and fruits.
By these and other such statements, the *caryāvrata* (observance of conduct) is described as that which is to be performed by undertaking the *vidyāvrata* (observance of knowledge).

As for whichever woman or man requests the *caryāvrata*, one should visualize her as Vajravārāhī, or Nairātmyā, or as the family deity (*kuladevī*) corresponding to the fall of the flower; and the man as any one of the forms such as Saṃvara-Hevajra. Then, having caused the wisdom-deity (*jñānadevatā*)—brought forth by rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart—to enter into her or him.
Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel, Amitābha is the nature of the earrings,
Ratneśa is in the necklace, and Vairocana is said to be in the hand.
Amogha is situated on the girdle.

Having spoken thus, one should instantly visualize—in that order—the wheel, earring, necklace, armlet, and girdle as being the forms of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasambhava, Vairocana, and Amoghasiddhi. Then, having caused the respective *jñānasattvas* brought from there to enter into them, and having resolved with conviction that the mudrās such as the wheel—which have been transformed from Akṣobhya and the others—are indeed of the very nature of Akṣobhya and the rest, [one recites]:
*oṃ dhara dhara dhāraya dhāraya marda marda vajradhṛk phaṭ svāhā*.

Having recited this mantra three times, one should place the *cakrī* on the head of that [person] or another, while reciting the verse beginning with "gr̥hṇa" (*gr̥hṇeti*). In the case of a female, having substituted the reading "vīra" with "devī," one should install it while reciting it.
Then, having recited three times: "Oṃ vajradharma samayas tvaṃ hulu hulu ārolik phaṭ svāhā," one should place the two earrings on the ears.
"Oṃ vajrasūrya tamovidhamana samayas tvam ahaṃ ratnadhṛk phaṭ svāhā.
Having recited this three times, he should place the necklace upon the neck.
"Oṃ śāśvata paramaśāśvata ehy ehi jinajik phaṭ svāhā."
Thus, having recited [the mantra] three times, one should place two *rucaka* ornaments like bracelets on the hands.

Then, having recited "Oṃ phu phu hi hi hi prajñādhṛk phaṭ svāhā" three times, one should place the girdle (*mekhalā*) on the hips. Immediately after [addressing her as] "O Goddess" (*devī*), or immediately after "O Heroine" (*vīrā*), according to the sequence, one should [visualize her] as the female consort (*cakrī*) in the form of Akṣobhya; these are the two earrings (*kuṇḍala*) of Vāgvajra.
"Take the necklace of Ratnasambhava," "the bracelet whose nature is eternal [Śāśvata]," and "the girdle of Amoghasiddhi"— having inserted these, one should recite "take [them]" and so forth.

Now, if a woman or a man who has attained the capacity for the [four] visions and so forth desires to undertake the *vīracaryā* vow for the sake of others, one should visualize her in the form of Vajravārāhī and him in the form of Saṃvara, as being of one essence with the Jñānasattva. One should then resolve upon the wheel and other [ornaments] as before, and likewise regard the garland of severed heads and so forth as having the nature of their respective mantra-deities. Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Having thus recited this three times, one should likewise place the wheel;
and as for the five skull-cups which consist of the nature of the five Buddhas, it is said: "Vairocani" is the mantra for one whose head is adorned with skull-cups.
Thus,
here the skull-cup also has the form of a wheel.
Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus, the two earrings are consecrated by reciting [the mantra] three times;
as it has been said:
"The earring that adorns the ear is [consecrated] with the seven-syllable mantra."
Thus,
with the root mantra of Vajravārāhī,
or with the mantra beginning "Oṃ sarvabuddha... and so forth, one should recite [the mantra] three times over a necklace.
As it has been said:
"The mantra of Vajravārāhī, adorned with a necklace upon the neck."
Thus:
"Oṃ hanamahi svāhā hūṃ vauṣaṭ he hūṃ hūṃ ho phaṭ haṃ. This mantra, recited three times, [is applied to] two bracelets, as it has been stated.
With six [syllables] of the armor-mantra, this mudrā, which beautifies the limbs, is formed by the hero.
Thus: *oṃ vaṃ hāṃ yoṃ hrīṃ moṃ hroṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
Having recited this mantra three times over the girdle, as it has been said:
With the mantra "ṣaḍyoginī," he made the girdle his ornament.
Thus: *Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā*.
Having recited this three times, [he should place] a garland of fifty skulls around his neck.
As it has been said:
"The heart-mantra of the deity is indeed a garland adorned with fifty [syllables]."
Thus:
*Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mantra, recited three times, is for the lower garment and the tiger skin. As it has been said:
The supreme [form] of the Ḍākinī of all Buddhas is one who wears garments of skin.
Thus,

with the thirty-six mantras beginning with *oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* and ending with *oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, the vessel for drinking the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) is recited over three times and placed in the hand. As it has been said:
The yoginīs of the entire wheel [hold] a skull-cup filled with mantra-liquor.
Thus:
having consecrated the *khaṭvāṅga* and the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) three times with the root mantra of the Blessed One, one should take them up with the verse beginning "Take [them]," and so forth.

With the root mantra of Śrī Saṃvara, one should recite [the mantra] three times over the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), the necklace suspended from the neck, the ornaments, the vajra, the crown made of thieves' hair, the double-wrapped hair-braids (*caḍorī*), the ashes, the armlets, the anklets, and the *ghurghurā* [bells], each in its respective place.
As it has been said:
"That which is the hero of the root mantra, conceived as the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) and so forth."
Thus it is said.

(219) In that regard, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) should be made with one string; the girdle (*mekhalā*) with eight strings, which is the same for women’s waists; and the necklace (*āhāra*) with sixteen or twenty-five strings. As it has been stated:
The sacred thread should consist of one strand; the girdle, eight strands;
the belt is known to have sixteen; and the garland, twenty-five.
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) may be made of human sinew or hair;
herein, the wheel and other [ornaments] should be fashioned from bone as appropriate, along with the vajra-ornaments.
That one [portion] is for the crest; thus it has been said.
Having made five finger-breadths into sections, it is worn upon the crown.
Thus,
the other ornaments located on the ears, neck, heart, secret place, and arms are to be arranged so that they appear beautiful.
The thirty-six mantras and the two root mantras have been described by us in the *Śrīsaṃvarābhisamayopāyikā*.
The vow of the heroic conduct (*vīracaryāvratam*) itself is called the practice of the vow of the crown prince (*yauvarājyavratacaryā*),
and it is also referred to as the vow of the Vajrakapāli conduct (*vajrakapālicaryāvratam*) in the *Śrīsampuṭatantra*.
Following that, one should worship with the five mudrās and so forth.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for bestowing the vow of conduct.
25. The Ritual Procedure for Prophecy:

Then, having composed himself in the posture of the Tathāgata, he places his left fist at his heart with the edge of his robe tucked into it, and [assumes] the right hand in the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) mudrā.
I, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, prophesy for you,
having extracted you from the miserable states of existence, for the sake of the ultimate pacification of cyclic existence.

Reciting the mantra, "O [Name]vajra, you are the samaya for the accomplishment of the Tathāgata; bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he should prophesy the disciple’s form as that of a Tathāgata corresponding to where the flower fell.
It should be believed that whoever is thus prophesied is prophesied for perfect enlightenment by all the Tathāgatas.

Thus is the procedure for the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). These—the knowledge (*vidyā*), vajra-conduct (*vajracaryā*), vows (*vrata*), and prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*)—are in some cases designated as "empowerment" (*abhiṣeka*) at the beginning of the tantras.
26. The Procedure for Authorization (*ānujñā-vidhi*).

Thereafter, following that fourth [initiation] with the words "likewise again," one should then grant the authorization to the disciple whose defilements have been removed by the initiation of the awakening mind (bodhicitta).
Thus, according to the *Sampuṭa*, while reciting "Oṃ vajrahetu maṃ," one should place the syllable *bhrūṃ* on a seat somewhere in front of the disciple's seat as the Dharma-wheel with the right hand.

Saying "Oṃ vajrabhāṣa raṃ," while reciting the first vowel (*ā*), he places in the left hand a conch born from the syllable *āḥ*; while reciting the first vowel, he places a book; and while reciting the final vowel, he places a bell born from the final vowel. As he causes him to ring that bell, [he says]: "Everything has the characteristic of space, and space is also without characteristics.
Through union with the equality of space, the equality of all things is clearly manifest as supreme."
From this day forward, by the mere arising of the thought [of awakening], turn the wheel of Dharma;
for you have completely filled the unsurpassed conch of Dharma in every direction.
Thus he should say:

"As the foremost of all, you shall clearly and directly perceive through meditation the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena by virtue of their being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*); you too, therefore, act accordingly. Now, moreover, by means of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), turn the wheel of Dharma"—thus the bell indicates. Having thus granted general permission, in order to grant specific permission, one should visualize the disciple in the form of Vairocana and so forth, and [say]:
"For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, in all worlds, in every way..."
Just as you have done, turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of disciplining the universe.
Your very self is the nature of wisdom and skillful means; like a wish-fulfilling jewel, remain unwearying and free from attachment, and now act for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus, by substituting the word *dharma* with the words *vajra*, *ratna*, *padma*, and *karma*, one should grant permission through five recitations.
Having prostrated, he should say:
"I shall act exactly as the Lord commands."
Thus ends the procedure for permission (anujñāvidhi).
Next is the procedure for breath-control (śvāsavidhi).
Holding a parasol over his head and having performed a circumambulation,
he should speak with palms joined at the entrance of the mandala, lowering the parasol as he does so.
This disciple, having been thus informed, shall become a bearer of the tantra.
Thus,
having thus entreated the Lord of the Maṇḍala and set aside the parasol elsewhere, he should speak words that reach the heart of the disciple:
"Now, you have become a master of the maṇḍala, a bearer of the mantra and tantra."
It is esteemed by the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the deities.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you should diligently draw the maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure, and practitioners should be applied to the tantra.
Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today itself completely liberated from all evils and well-established.
There is no further falling away for you from this vehicle of great bliss;
the suffering of existence has ceased for you, for the sake of the ultimate accomplishment of liberation from cyclic existence.
O Venerable One, you have today been consecrated by all the Buddhas together with the Holders of the Vajra;
it is certain that you are the sovereign lord of the great kingdom of the three realms.
There is no other evil in the three realms equal to dispassion;
therefore, you must never again practice the state of being free from desire for sensual pleasures.
"Enjoy yourself with all objects of desire, free from fear from any quarter;
the five meats and the nectar are to be consumed—this, O Rākṣasa, is the other commitment."
One must not commit the taking of life; one must not abandon a jewel of a woman. One must not forsake one's teacher; the vow is difficult to transgress.
There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by a mind endowed with wisdom and skillful means;
do not fear, for there is no sin in you, according to the word of the Tathāgata.
Thus, fashion the diamond of mental clarity; embrace this own commitment (*svasamaya*) which bestows inexhaustible bliss!
For in this world of fleeting happiness, you have now attained the eternal state equal to Vajrasattva.

Moreover, this is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): that one who has been consecrated according to the ritual is attended by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with minds as clear as those of a beloved son, solely for the sake of their welfare. This is the procedure for providing consolation.
28. The Procedure for the Consecration of Another:
And the disciple, having thus received the consecration and being comforted, becomes joyful and thinks, "I shall act in this way."
Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life as well;
today I am born into the family of the Buddhas, and I am now truly a son of the Buddha.
Thus he should say.

And he should respectfully give to the guru, according to his ability, sacrificial fees consisting of elephants, horses, jewels, gold, silver, clothing, ornaments, cows, buffaloes, male and female slaves, laborers, and so forth, as well as his beloved wife, daughters, sons, and others;
and he should perform offerings, fire-oblations, communal feasts, and other such rites.

"Completely liberated" means being freed from the restriction of evil deeds; "well-established" means being established in the certainty of a happy rebirth; "ceased" means the attainment of the *dharmakāya*.
"Ultimately" refers to existence (*bhava*) which is without end, the *saṃbhogakāya* being eternal through its lack of exhaustion.
"Vajra" refers to the indivisible clarity of mind toward the guru, the Buddhas, and so forth.
Your own commitment (*svasamaya*) consists of your own deity and so forth.
Although you have been born into a world of little happiness and much suffering, you have attained faultless great bliss and permanence.

Here, in order to illuminate the natural purity of the disciple—who possesses the nature of the Tathāgata as indicated by the falling of the flower—the consecration with the garland upon the head is performed.
The water-consecration is for the purpose of instilling the fitness for washing away the impurity of ignorance;
the crown-consecration is for the purpose of applying the refinement of the seal of the Tathāgata and for the sake of the fitness for the manifestation of the *uṣṇīṣa*.
The binding of the hero’s band is for the purpose of uprooting the enemies such as the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is an auxiliary to the consecration of the crown.

In some places this is designated as the "separate consecration," while in others the "binding of the fillet" (paṭṭabandha) is not mentioned, because its purpose is accomplished by the crown consecration (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*) due to a particular intention. The vajra consecration is for the sake of instilling the capacity for the arising of indivisible gnosis.

The empowerment by means of the sounding bell, which indicates the *dharmodayā* (source of phenomena), is for the purpose of awakening [the disciple] through the sovereign power of the arising of non-dual gnosis—the inseparability of unsurpassed emptiness and compassion.
