Because it possesses that sovereignty, it is called the "empowerment of sovereignty" (*ādhipatyābhiṣeka*). The name-empowerment (*nāmābhiṣeka*) is for the purpose of implanting the seed-syllable of the name appropriate for the future station of a Lord of Sages.

Furthermore, these five [rites], beginning with the sprinkling of water, should be understood as being of the nature of the five wisdoms—namely, the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*, equality, discernment, accomplishment, and mirror-like wisdom—respectively, through the nourishment of their seeds. It has also been stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* that "the sprinkling of water is of the nature of mirror-like wisdom," and that "Akṣobhya is also of the nature of mirror-like wisdom.

From this point onward, the "vajra-samaya" consists in the binding of the retention of the vajra, which is of that same nature, by means of the restriction that one must strive to attain the awakening of the union of purity.

The *samaya* of sound and terminology (*sadhvanighaṇṭāsamaya*) is for the purpose of establishing [the disciple] in the realization of suchness (*tathatā*), which is the source for teaching the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*).

The *mudrā-samaya* is for the purpose of instilling the firm capacity for the nature of a perfectly awakened Buddha (*sambuddha*), whose essence consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) and is characterized by great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* that the consecration of a perfectly awakened Buddha (*sambuddhābhiṣeka*) is precisely the *mudrā-samaya*, as it is encompassed by these two *samayas*. However, in other tantras, a triad of *samayas* is taught as the prerequisites for the master’s consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*).

And as it was stated previously: "With both hands," and so forth. Since the capacity for washing away impurities exists in both systems of the *samaya*, there is no contradiction. Just as on the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the great Bodhisattvas who do not turn back are consecrated by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

Likewise, this [disciple] as well, surrounded by the three times and by those [preceptors], is consecrated by the Guru—through immeasurable assemblies of sentient beings and limitless teachings and so forth—to act as a master in the Dharma-kingdom of the triple world; thus there is the *ācāryābhiṣeka* (master-consecration) and the *avaivartikābhiṣeka* (irreversible-consecration), like that of those who are irreversible.
And in this way, the seed of irreversibility is planted.

For this very reason, with respect to that, it is called the *avaivartyābhiṣeka* (consecration for the irreversible) and the *avivartābhiṣeka* (consecration of non-retrogression); thus it is termed the *avaivartyaseka* and the *avivartaseka*.
Therefore,
the notion that "the one called the Ācārya is here said to be threefold by means of the secret vajra-knowledges" belongs only to those of poor intellect.

The recitation of mantras is for the sake of being free from obstacles, for implanting the seeds of accomplishments such as peace (*śānti*), and for purifying the field of ultimate mantra-accomplishment.
The ointment (*añjana*) is for the arising of the superknowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*) through the removal of the film of ignorance.
And the mirror initiation (*darpaṇābhiṣeka*) is for establishing the impression of perceiving the manifold universe like a reflection by means of that [superknowledge].
The "arrow-shooting" is for the purpose of planting the seed for the penetration of the extremely subtle objective field of the *dharmadhātu* by means of the victory over the four Māras.

The secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) is for the purpose of making faith and wisdom into a field, for the purpose of guarding the pledge (*samaya*), and for the purpose of purifying speech. Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that in which there is preeminent knowledge; it refers to the external consort. Knowledge in her is the mind purified through the departure of conceptual construction, which is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
The initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*);

that very knowledge, when attained through stainless purity, is the fourth initiation. These two are also called initiations because of the sprinkling (*secanāt*) by means of the essence of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) upon the mind.

Connected to this very point is the *vidyāvrata*: because wisdom alone is the direct means for the attainment of the inexhaustible abundance of true bliss, it must not be abandoned even during the initial stages. When one performs all actions with skillful means while remaining in a non-conceptual state—that is, with a non-conceptual disposition—it is the most supreme of all vows.

Thus, according to the statement of Vajraḍāka: "What is the use of other vows? there is the *vajravratam* (vajra-vow), which is intended to strictly enjoin one to the vow of the bodhicitta consisting of the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*).
Furthermore, since the realization of bodhicitta does not occur without conduct (*caryā*), there is the *caryāvratam* (conduct-vow) for the purpose of instruction.
This has three types.
Among these, the first is devoted to the application of the three internal mudrās;
and so it has been said:
"The khaṭvāṅga is the form of the deity, and the prajñā is conceived as the ḍamaru."
Thus ends the *Mantrapānakaroṭaka*.
And thus:

[this section] teaches three things—the deity’s body, the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) of the *caṇḍālī* in its radiant form, and the conventional bodhicitta which is the basis for the experience of non-dual great bliss.
The second [section] is devoted to the application of generating the fivefold pure dharmadhātu-knowledge and so forth, for both the yoginī and the one observing the conduct-vow (*caryāvratī*).

The third [type] pertains to a yogin or yoginī who, possessing the power of the fourfold vision, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and so forth, is devoted to accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings and has transcended the world; it consists of the application of the arising of the bodhicitta—which is composed of emptiness and great compassion—as a means to support all internal ornaments.
Thus it is said in the *Yoginīsañcāra-tantra*:
"First, the yogin, being well-composed, should diligently generate the Power (*śakti*)."
Later, having acquired the necessary capacity, he undertook the practice of the vow without desire for reward.
The practice of the five colors is conceived as being of a single color;
with a non-conceptual mind focused on the one, one should enjoy the five objects of desire.
Thus, the knower of Śrī Heruka, who fulfills all hopes and possesses great wisdom,
practices the excellent vow of non-dual gnosis.
For one engaged in the observance of the conduct-vow, yoga should be known as well-determined.
Thus,

the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) is given in order to illuminate that you are fit for the sequence of realizing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) which does not transcend the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
For instance, "the earth" (*bhūḥ*) refers to the foundation consisting of the surrounding spheres of wind and so forth, as well as the netherworld (*pātāla*).
*Bhuvaḥ* refers to the mortal world (*bhūr-martyaloka*).

*Svaḥ* refers to the heavenly realm (*svarga*), extending up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Since you are the pledge (*samaya*)—that is, the one who, through your capacity, shall realize the reality of that intrinsic nature by means of the sequence of the stages beginning with *pramuditā*—the meaning of "You are the pledge of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*" is an authorization: "Having accomplished success according to the ritual rules, perform the welfare of sentient beings through the teaching of the Dharma and so forth."

Even while enjoying sensual pleasures, one is liberated from all obscurations; "you are a Buddha this very day"—this is the consolation (*āśvāsa*) arising from the intention to provide the fitness for nourishment through the entry into the mandala and so forth. These five, beginning with the *vajravrata*, are authorized by some immediately after the master initiation (*ācāryaseka*) and immediately after the knowledge initiation (*vidyāseka*) for those who are satisfied with each respective [initiation] alone. Furthermore, the mantra, collyrium, mirror, and arrow-throwing are also [authorized] immediately after the knowledge initiation.
In some cases, even after the wisdom-consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*), the knowledge-vow (*vidyāvrata*) is not mentioned;

in other cases, the mantra-vow and so forth, the conduct-vow (*caryāvrata*), the general permission (*sāmānyānujñā*), the three pledges (*samaya*), and the fitness (*bhavyatā*) are not stated. This is because, according to the requirements, these are intended to be included within the meanings of the respective other consecrations.
In some instances, the permission and the assurance (*āśvāsa*) are included within the "irreversible" (*avivarta*) stage.
In this [work], however, everything has been stated separately.
As for what was said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara Tantra*:
"The first [initiation] is by means of water-sprinkling; the second is from the crown-initiation (*mauliseka*)."
The third is through the vajra-consecration, and the fourth is through self-sovereignty.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] with the fifth [consecration] by name, and the sixth is that of the Perfectly Awakened One (sambuddha).
The seventh is the vase consecration (kalaśaseka), the eighth is the secret consecration (guhyaseka), and the ninth is from the wisdom consecration (prajñābhiṣeka).
Through the yoga of the vajra of reality, he should bestow the vajra-vow upon all;
the Teacher himself grants the prophecy—this is the sequence of the ritual for empowerment.
Thus [it is said].

In that regard, since the sprinkling with a garland (*mālāseka*) serves as the cause for the sprinkling with water (*udakaseka*) and so forth, and because it should be understood—according to the statements in other tantras—that the mantras and so forth function respectively as the prerequisites (*parikara*) for the master’s sprinkling (*ācāryaseka*), the fourth sprinkling, and occasionally others, they are not explicitly mentioned here.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śrīsamāja*:
In this tantra, the consecration is established as threefold:
the first is the vase consecration, and the second is the secret consecration.
The third is indeed the gnosis of wisdom (prajñājñāna), and the fourth is likewise that again.
Thus it is said; and in the Śrīsampuṭa:
"And that initiation is fourfold; first is the vase initiation (kalaśābhiṣeka)."
The second [empowerment] is from the secret empowerment.
The third is the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna), and the fourth is that same [wisdom] once again.
Thus,
it is said in the *Dvikalpatantra*:
"The master, the secret, and the wisdom [consort], and the fourth is likewise."
Thus [it is said].

In that regard, the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) is sixfold due to the distinctions among the water, crown, and vajra-lord preceptors (*ācārya*). This is because one is consecrated with vases by means of the vidyās such as Tathāgatalocanā and others in every case;

and because the preceptor consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is especially superior due to its being the most excellent sprinkling. Furthermore, it is stated that the "seventh" is the vase consecration (*kalaśaseka*).

Since the fivefold [initiation] beginning with the water initiation is taught as the cause for the arising of that master’s initiation, it is entirely consistent that this is called the "master's consecration.
Thus, this is the procedure for the initiation of another;
[next is] the procedure for one's own initiation.
If one has oneself violated the commitments (*samaya*), one should likewise receive such an empowerment as was prescribed for the procedure of the master’s entry (at 231).
However, this applies only if the true guru resides in a very distant place or in a region inaccessible due to obstacles such as difficult paths; otherwise, it does not.

But always, by way of formal undertaking, through the yoga of one’s chosen deity whose essence is the single flavor of wisdom and means, within the mentally constructed mandala, one should receive from the Lord of the Mandala the water empowerment and so forth—up to the secret, wisdom-knowledge, and fourth empowerments, and up to the final breath—as the procedure for one’s own empowerment.

30. Regarding the procedure for consecration (*ābhiṣeka*), this Vajrasattva-vow-holder has two categories of downfalls: root downfalls and gross downfalls. These have been explained in detail in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*. In the event of faults such as disrespect toward the guru, one should give gifts and food according to one's ability, and having first performed confession in the presence of the guru, one should take the vow (*saṃvara*) again as before.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for consecration, together with its ancillaries and the traditional recitation.
